name: Meal prep
lead: Meal prep is the practice of planning and cooking meals in advance, often a week at a time, and storing them in portioned containers [1]. In fitness and appearance communities it is used to control calories and protein and to avoid unplanned eating.

Wikipedia notes people use it to lose weight, build muscle or keep a healthy lifestyle, and links frequent home cooking with lower type 2 diabetes risk [1]. A small published program study reported that a six-week group-based advanced meal prep course improved cooking attitudes, behaviours and body composition [2].

paras: Fully cooked meals are made ahead to standardise portions and are often stored in small labelled, dated containers [1]. Related services include meal kits and meal delivery companies.

Pre-cooked food can grow bacteria if stored improperly or eaten too late, and plastic containers can shed microplastics, particularly when microwaved [1]. Wikipedia also notes that over-structured prepping can lead to rigidity or a food rut [1].
Meal prep is discussed alongside bodybuilding-style diets and low-carbohydrate eating, with users asking about prep ideas and meal prep companies in forum threads [3][4].

A six-week group-based advanced quantity meal prep program reported improvements in cooking attitudes, behaviours and body composition [2]. A pilot of a community meal-kit service in Washington DC studied vegetable intake barriers rather than appearance [5]. Evidence specific to looksmaxxing outcomes is limited.

card.summary: Cook ahead, portion it out; a habit tool for hitting diet targets, with small studies linking it to better habits.
card.note: Food-safety storage matters for pre-cooked meals.

quick.overview:
Meal prep means cooking and portioning meals in advance, usually weekly. Fitness communities use it to keep calories and protein on target.

Studies are small. One six-week program reported better cooking habits and body composition.
quick.mechanism: Having portioned meals ready reduces decision-making and unplanned eating, which supporters say makes a diet easier to follow.
quick.risks: Stored cooked food can grow bacteria if kept or reheated improperly, and some plastic containers can shed microplastics when heated.
